rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the evidence instead of dressing one product launch as an industry turn. Its best line, "Deel's AI flags contractor-classification risk across 150 countries - but won't say how accurate it is," is a clean reporter frame built directly from the update. B has useful material, but "Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire. AI Is Moving It to the Moment of the Decision." invents a market shift the facts do not prove. That is how a decent angle set gets extra homework from an editor.
gaps_in_A: "a budget question for HR teams' outside counsel" is plausible but still speculative without a named customer or spend-displacement data; A admits the proof gap, which saves it from slop.
"any adoption or usage figures since the rollout is automatic" overstates the facts. The update says the tool is included for existing customers, not that rollout or usage is automatic.

The set underuses the $12B/private-company fact. A cleaner business-model angle could ask whether bundling AI compliance protects platform retention, but A only partially gets there through the outside-counsel budget frame.
gaps_in_B: "Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire. AI Is Moving It to the Moment of the Decision." is the biggest foul: the update says the tool checks risk as a company hires, not that global compliance historically happened after hiring.
"Deel's launch is the first concrete product the reporter can point to as evidence of the shift" invents a category claim. No comparison set, no competitor data, no analyst proof.
"they raise a pointed question about the competitive pressure driving the launch" overreads the lawsuit. The facts support juxtaposition, not causation or launch pressure.

"That's a Bet on Moat Over Margin" is a sharp business headline, but it outruns the disclosed pricing facts. We only know existing customers get it included; we do not know new-customer pricing, margins, or monetization strategy.
